title: Beef and Ale Stew
subtitle: Slow-braised beef shin with root vegetables and dark ale
excerpt: Chunks of beef shin braised low and slow in dark ale with carrots, onions, and herbs until the meat is tender enough to fall apart. A proper British stew, best made the day before.

recipe.sourceNotes: Beef stewed slowly in ale or wine is a tradition shared across Northern Europe. The British version typically uses a dark ale or stout and relies on root vegetables for sweetness rather than the aromatics of the French daube. Beef shin is the ideal cut: it is inexpensive, full of collagen, and becomes very tender after 2 to 3 hours of gentle braising. The collagen dissolves into gelatin as it cooks, giving the sauce its body and lip-coating richness. The stew genuinely improves overnight in the fridge: the fat solidifies and can be skimmed, and the flavours deepen.

recipeTools.notes: A large, heavy casserole dish with a lid for the long braise.

content.text: Brown the beef in batches in a very hot pan: do not crowd the pan or the beef will steam rather than colour. Good browning is what gives the stew its deep, savoury base note. The stew can go in the oven (160 C) or stay on the hob at the lowest setting. Oven braising gives more even heat. The beef is done when a piece breaks apart easily when pressed.

Heat the oven to 160 C / fan 140 C / gas 3. Pat the beef dry. Season and dust lightly with flour. Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a large casserole over high heat. Brown the beef in batches for 3 to 4 minutes per batch until well coloured on all sides. Remove to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the remaining oil. Cook the onion, carrot, and celery for 8 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree. Cook for 2 minutes. Pour in the stout and scrape up any browned bits. Add the stock, Worcestershire sauce, bay leaves, thyme, and rosemary.

Return the beef to the casserole. The liquid should come about three-quarters up the beef. Bring to a simmer. Cover with a tight-fitting lid and transfer to the oven. Cook for 2.5 to 3 hours until the beef is very tender and breaks apart easily. Taste and adjust seasoning. Remove the herb sprigs. Serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.
